items.title: Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says
items.summary_raw:
High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels

The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.

The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

items.title: US datacenter demand spurs increased fossil fuel pipeline projects as rules are discarded
items.summary_raw:
Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues

Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.

The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

items.title: Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks
items.summary_raw:
What are the relationships and dominant interests in play, as the summit kicks off after a bitter row over its hosting?

Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. About 53 percent of Air Force aircraft are over 30 years old, and 55 percent have exceeded their projected service life. The F-16, B-52, KC-135 and F-35 fleets face parts problems, and 36 planned engine repairs on B-52 and KC-135 aircraft were postponed in fiscal 2024 and 2025 due to parts shortages. The Air Force has requested about $4.25 billion for parts supply in fiscal 2027.

items.title: The Turkish Ruse: Smoke on the High Seas?
items.summary_raw:
Pay attention here please because this topic is a real MEGO – My Eyes Glaze Over – but it’s important to Greece, and Cyprus, and speaks to the doublespeak chicanery that is the modus operandi of Turkey. Apparently they don’t teach geography in Turkey either, at least not for politicians and officials who can’t read a map unless it’s the unreasonable facsimile of the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean under the dubious Blue Homeland Doctrine. Under that, Turkey declares a vast maritime jurisdiction of roughly 178,379 square miles in those waters which are Greek. Turkey believes calling something by what it wants and staking a claim means the territory or waters are Turkish, even if they are not. Turkey also asserted rights to continental shelves and Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) near its coastline.

US President Donald Trump says Israel would no longer exist if he had allowed Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon, while defending his military campaign against Tehran.

Speaking at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Friday, Trump  said: “If I allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, today there would be no Israel,” he said.

“Israel would’ve been wiped off the face of the earth,” Trump added, according to Al Jazeera.

items.title: New Turkish NAVTEX for Underwater Studies for the Pipeline with the Pseudo-State
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – Turkey issued a new NAVTEX from the Antalya station concerning scientific research and underwater studies to be conducted at 12 specified coordinates in the Mediterranean between October 26 and December 31, 2026, in the maritime area between Turkey and occupied Cyprus. According to the website of Turkish state television TRT, the studies will be carried out by the vessels R/V Denar Pathfinder, Denar Echo, Denar Explorer, and Kırıcı. The NAVTEX calls on mariners passing through the area to maintain a safe distance from the vessels carrying out the work. The TRT Haber website writes that the planned natural gas pipeline between Turkey and the  pseudo-state aims to deliver natural gas from Turkey to the island in the future and strengthen the pseudo-state’s security of energy supply. It is maintained that, following the construction of the underwater water-supply pipeline from Turkey to the pseudo-state, the project is considered one of the important steps toward improving energy infrastructure between “the two countries.” The NAVTEX announcement stated that the notice will expire on December 31, 2026.

items.title: Greece’s Electricity Exports Hit New Record
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - Despite rising electricity prices internationally and across the region due to the energy crisis, Greece has maintained its competitive advantage over neighboring countries, increasing its electricity exports to the region. According to data from the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO) and the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT), electricity exports rose sharply in the first eight months of 2026, making a significant positive contribution to the country's trade balance. Net electricity exports (exports minus imports) reached 6.1 terawatt-hours (TWh) between January and August, according to IPTO, and its Chairman and CEO Manos Manousakis told ANA-MPA that, "this development is the result of our national energy strategy to harness our abundant domestic renewable resources, namely solar and wind energy, as well as the systematic development of our electricity infrastructure.”

The post Greece’s Electricity Exports Hit New Record appeared first on The National Herald.

The event brought together distinguished representatives of government, business, academia, energy, finance, and the maritime industry for an evening of substantive dialogue on the evolving U.S.-Greece strategic partnership and the growing importance of energy security, infrastructure development, investment, and technological innovation. The gathering underscored Greece's increasingly significant role as a strategic energy and infrastructure hub connecting the United States, Europe, and the Eastern Mediterranean, while highlighting opportunities to transform transatlantic cooperation into meaningful commercial partnerships.

items.title: How rare earth elements can be upcycled from magnets
items.summary_raw: Technology that enables the recovery of rare earth elements such as neodymium from magnets is being developed in the NEO-CYCLE project in Germany with researchers from the Fraunhofer IKTS and TU Bergakademie Freiberg. Such magnets are used, among other things, in electric vehicles and wind turbines, and through these new technologies, can be upcycled in Europe for other industries, including pharmaceuticals and the hydrogen economy.

items.title: The next global pandemic could be brewing on a mink farm in Utah – and little is being done to stop it | George Monbiot
items.summary_raw:
Mink farms are the perfect petri dishes for deadly flu strains to emerge. Yet officials appear to be protecting business interests over human lives

Could this be ground zero? Could it be the spot where the next pandemic begins? It’s certainly a candidate, not least because the chain of events that could trigger a plague far worse than Covid-19 looks like the opening sequence of a disaster movie. A really bad disaster movie, in which the levels of carelessness and turpitude defy belief.

A report by the investigative news service ProPublica reveals that bird flu has been raging in a mink farm in Utah since August, and it appears next to nothing has been done by public officials. In 2023, I warned in the Guardian that mink farms could scarcely be better designed to generate lethal plagues. This is for three reasons: mink are fed on the offcuts of chickens, cows and other farm animals, in which new viral variants often develop; mink readily host both avian and human flu virus

Bluetongue, a viral disease that affects sheep, cattle and goats, can cause fever, lesions, stillbirths and death. The tongue may go blue and protrude from the mouth.

items.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying
items.summary_raw:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.

This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.

items.title: Control of Britain’s 39m smart meters passes to non-profit startup
items.summary_raw:
The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays

Control over Great Britain’s 39m smart meters has passed to a non-profit startup after its former owner presided over more than a decade of spiralling costs and delays in the troubled network.

The company owned by crisis-hit outsourcing firm Capita has promised a “seamless transition” to its not-for-profit successor, which will take over running the data network connecting the smart meters from this week.

items.title: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean
items.summary_raw:
A Guardian investigation has found that despite a recommendation to slow down, leading shipping companies continue to travel above advised speeds in a key habitat for cetaceans

Marine biologist Alice Barbarioli waits with her camera trained on the horizon. A few minutes earlier, the hydrophone beneath the Pelagos research vessel detected codas – the sequence of clicks sperm whales use to communicate.

The sperm whale reveals its head and dorsal fin as those onboard the vessel in the Pelagos sanctuary, a conservation area established to protect marine mammals in the north-western Mediterranean, rush to take photos and note the rhythm of its breathing. After a few minutes, the animal arches its back, and begins to head back into the depths of the sea. They wait to catch a glimpse of its tail.

items.title: Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn
items.summary_raw:
UN-backed report finds even temporary rises above Paris agreement target could cause harm to glaciers and polar ice sheets

Earth’s icy regions face such dangerous melting that global heating should be brought back below 1C after an inevitable period of overshooting global temperature targets, a UN report has found.

Permanent and widespread losses of snow and ice expose a “persistent myth” that overshooting the 1.5C target of the Paris climate agreement – to 2C or 3C – could be manageable or even preferable to urgent cuts to emissions, the report found.

items.title: Saudi Arabia condemns strike on Qatar’s LNG tanker
items.summary_raw:
Saudi Arabia condemns strike on Qatar’s LNG tanker

Saudi Arabia has condemned the attack on Qatar’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Mayeda and backed measures to protect Qatari vessels and international trade.

In a statement posted on X, the Saudi foreign ministry reiterated its “rejection of all violations that threaten the security and safety of maritime navigation and global energy supplies”.

It urged the international community to act immediately to uphold international law and “ensure maritime security and the safety of international trade”.

The Al Mayeda, owned and operated by the Qatar Gas Transport Company, was struck in the Gulf earlier today.

items.summary_raw:

Iran had approved the voyage just hours earlier after Pakistan negotiated safe passage. The circumstances of the attack remain unclear.

All 25 crew are safe, including 6 Indians. Nakilat: the vessel is still operational.
